title: The old plane trees
hookLine: at his country house Seneca finds the trees he planted grown old, and so is he

cards: Seneca goes out to his house in the country. The walls are cracking, and he scolds the man who manages the place: what are you spending the money on? The manager says, very politely, that it isn't his fault.
The house is old. Seneca walks on, a little irritated, to the plane trees by the path, and finds them bare and knotted. Has nobody been looking after these?
The manager swears he's been digging and watering them. And then Seneca remembers who planted them.

teach.h: THE HOUSE HE BUILT IS CRUMBLING.
teach.b: Wherever he turns, Seneca says at the start of letter twelve, he sees signs of his age. The house is crumbling, and he built it.
The plane trees are gnarled, their branches twisted and dry, and he planted them himself and saw their first leaves. The trees are simply old. So, Seneca realizes, is he.
Then at the door he sees a frail old man and asks, rather rudely, who on earth that is. The old man answers: don't you know me? I'm Felicio, the son of your old manager.
You used to bring me little toys. I was your favorite. Seneca, who wrote this himself, lets the joke land on him.
Everything he complains about, he's part of. And then, instead of sinking, he turns.

teach.h: LOVE OLD AGE; IT HAS ITS SWEETNESS.
teach.b: Let us welcome old age and love it, he says. It's full of pleasure if you know how to use it. Fruit tastes best just as the season ends.
Youth is loveliest near its close. The last drink is the one the drinker savors. Every age has its own sweetness, and the late one has a kind all its own.

teach.h: A SHARED LIFE, NOT A TRAGEDY.
teach.b: Seneca and his trees, Seneca and Felicio, the house and the man who built it: not a tragedy.

how: Readers of Seneca's twelfth letter often take it as an invitation to notice their own aging with humor and affection rather than complaint.

games.q: you're Seneca. you've just scolded your manager about the cracked walls and bare trees, and he says: they're old, sir. what do you do?
o: remember you built the house and planted the trees, and laugh at yourself.
games.why: Seneca realizes the age is his own, and turns the moment into a lesson: love old age, it has its own sweetness.

practice: Look around for something that has aged alongside you: a chair, a book with a cracked spine, a ring, your own hands, or, if nothing is near, a tree outside a childhood home.
Look at the wear, the softness, the scratches, and what it has been through with you. See whether something like fondness comes, the way it came for Seneca once he stopped scolding.

wordCard.voice: Platanus. Latin for the plane tree Seneca planted himself, now gnarled with age, like the house and like him. Today's word.
